name: Lore
tagline: Who has worked on what in any public GitHub repo, with the pull requests behind it.
description:
Every project has people who have worked on a part of the code for months, and newcomers have no way to find them. CODEOWNERS files go stale, and the commit log shows who typed, not who reviewed or who answers questions about it.

Paste any public GitHub repo (owner/repo or a URL). Lore reads its last 12 months of pull requests, reviews, issues and comments, shows who has worked on which directories, and answers from that history with a PR or issue linked for every claim.

Lore describes public activity, not understanding. People also learn code by reading it, in chat and in private work, so Lore says "@x authored 5 and reviewed 3 of the 9 merged PRs in src/planner", never "only @x understands it". Every answer and draft is checked for claims like that, and for promises.

Ask: "Who has worked on the query planner?", "Why was the retry logic changed?", "I'm new, where should I start?" An agent picks queries over the history, shows each step it took, and answers with sources.

People by area: every area of the code, the people with the most activity in it, and the PRs behind each ranking.

Triage an issue: pick an open issue and get related past issues and PRs, who has worked on that area (never the issue's author), and a draft reply for you to edit. The draft makes no promises for you or the project, and nothing is posted anywhere.

Knowledge risk: areas with recent work where one active person has most of the public activity, each shown with its PRs and everyone on them.

How the ranking works: a merged PR counts 1.0, a review 0.6, a comment 0.2, and work counts half as much every 180 days. Lore reads public data only, keeps GitHub logins and no emails or names, and caches a loaded repo in your Anna storage for a day. GitHub allows 60 calls an hour without a token; one repo takes about 40. Lore reads files for the 30 most recent merged PRs. When a repo has more than that, or GitHub's limit cuts a load short, every result page says how much was read (for example "files read for 14 of 34 merged PRs").
